title.en: How smkabir.com stays up: releases, pointers and a failover that is still on paper

description.en: How the site is served from a homelab: R2 releases, two pointers, what happens when things fail, and the failover Worker that is designed but not built yet.

children.text: This site is static files served by two small nginx pods in a homelab. That is a deliberately boring design, and it makes the interesting question easy to state: what keeps the site up when something breaks? This post is the honest answer, including the part that does not exist yet.
content that lives outside the container image, release and pointer handling in object storage, pods that follow the pointer, verified publishing, rollback, and two replicas on different hosts.

the failover Worker that would serve a copy of the site from object storage when the whole homelab is unreachable. Until it exists, a power cut or an internet outage takes the site down. Everything below says which side of that line it is on.

fields.title: What is built, and what is only planned

fields.alt: A visitor reaches Cloudflare, then a tunnel, then a gateway in the cluster and two nginx pods. A sidecar in each pod polls an R2 bucket for the LATEST pointer. GitHub Actions uploads each release to the same bucket and moves LATEST, then VERIFIED.
fields.source:

cf: "Cloudflare edge"
tunnel: "Tunnel (cloudflared)"
gw: "Gateway (Cilium)"
pods: "Two blog pods" {
  nginx: "nginx"
  sync: "content-sync sidecar"
}
r2: "R2 bucket" { shape: cylinder }
ci: "GitHub Actions"

visitor -> cf: "HTTPS"
cf -> tunnel
tunnel -> gw
gw -> pods.nginx
pods.sync -> r2: "reads LATEST every 60 s"
ci -> r2: "uploads release,\nthen LATEST, then VERIFIED"

children.text: Nothing a visitor requests ever touches a database or a CMS. Pages are files. That is why the failure modes are few and the recovery is mostly "serve the previous files".
The content is not in the image
The container image holds nginx and a small sync program, and
. The site itself is a release: a folder in an object-storage bucket named after the build, such as
. Two small text files point into it:
names the release the pods should serve.
names the release that was actually seen serving correctly on the real site.
A new post is therefore not a deployment. There is no commit to the cluster repository, no image build and no rollout. A publish uploads a folder and moves a pointer.
How a pod follows the pointer
Each pod runs a sidecar that does the same small loop every 60 seconds:
. If it is empty, unreadable or not a plain id, do nothing and keep serving.
If it is already the live release, stop.
Download the release next to the live one, never over it.
says the same id as the folder.
Turn the release's redirect list into an nginx map using a strict character allow-list, so a bad entry can never inject configuration.
symlink in one atomic rename, ask nginx to reload, and delete everything but the live release and the previous one.
If any step fails, the previous release keeps serving. A visitor never sees a half-written site, and R2 being down means "keep what you have".
A release, from push to live
The publish job is one pipeline, and its order is the point:

Formatting, type checks, tests, a privacy scan (no GPS in images, no addresses or phone numbers), the build, and checks on the output: no inline scripts, correct language on every page, no drafts anywhere, every link resolves.
and re-verify the upload. A release is immutable: the same id with different content is refused, and re-running is a safe no-op.
The pods start syncing within a minute.
Wait until the public site reports the new id.
This polls the real URL for up to ten minutes.
, purge Cloudflare's cache and prune releases beyond the last twenty.
If step 4 never succeeds, the run fails loudly,
does not move, and the live site is untouched.
. They are separate because the thing you want to fall back to must never be a release nobody has looked at. A bad build can become
for a minute; it cannot become
only moves after the live site has reported that exact id. Any fallback reads
, so a fallback is never a gamble.
The sidecar rejects it; the previous release keeps serving.
only moves after the upload is verified.
Running pods keep serving what they have. A pod that has to start from scratch stays unready until it can fetch, so it takes no traffic.
The other serves. Two replicas on different hosts, at least one always available, and a rolling update never drops below that.
Pods are rescheduled. Spread is soft on purpose, so losing one host cannot leave a replica stuck pending.
The CI check cannot reach the site
does not move, the live site is untouched.
The whole homelab is unreachable (power, ISP)
The site is unreachable. Nothing here helps.
The failover that is not built yet

When the tunnel has no healthy connectors, Cloudflare answers with an error page, and its edge cache only helps on points of presence that happen to be warm. The design is a small Worker in front of the site:

fields.alt: Planned design: a Cloudflare Worker receives every request. If the origin answers normally the response is passed through. If the origin returns a server error, a tunnel error or times out after four seconds, the Worker reads VERIFIED from R2 and serves that release, with an X-Served-From header.

direction: right

visitor: "Visitor" { shape: person }
worker: "Failover Worker (planned)"
origin: "Homelab origin"
r2: "R2: VERIFIED release" { shape: cylinder }

visitor -> worker
worker -> origin: "try first, 4 s timeout"
worker -> r2: "only on 5xx, tunnel error or timeout"

children.text: goes straight to the origin; the Worker never invents a write.
It is the same bucket the pods read, so there is no second copy to keep in sync, and it never serves an unverified build.
The security headers come from one source file that renders both the nginx configuration and the Worker, so a mirrored response carries the same policy as an origin one.
, and an external uptime probe is meant to alert when it appears.
What still fails when the homelab is down:
publishing and previews. Reading, the resume, search and the feeds keep working, because they are files.
scale the deployment to zero through the cluster repository (Argo CD would undo a manual change within seconds), check the key pages and the header, then revert the commit.

It is on paper because the site only went live today and the failover is the next unit of work, not because it is hard. The release layout was chosen so that it is a small Worker and not a second system.
a manual workflow takes a build id, checks the release exists and is consistent, and rewrites
to it. The pods follow within a minute.
(the image): a tag is never moved. A fix is the next patch, and a rollback is reverting the commit that bumped the tag in the cluster repository.
What has been proven, and what has not
Proven in production in the last day:
uploads, pointer moves, pruning, and pods reading with a read-only token. The token that can write is a different token, held only by CI.
the content pipeline and the image release, including a vulnerability scan that stopped a release for a HIGH finding in a library the image did not need.
Argo CD sync, two ready pods on different hosts, the gateway route and the tunnel to the apex.
61 image checks (sidecar, nginx under the cluster's restrictions, redirects), 35 release-script checks, an end-to-end run of the real site through nginx, and unit tests.
Not proven: the failover Worker (it does not exist), a real power cut, and a sustained outage of the object store.
The wall CI hit on day one
The check in step 4 above failed for ten minutes with "last saw nothing". The site was serving the right release; the CI runner was being handed Cloudflare's

challenge page, because Bot Fight Mode treats a datacenter address as a bot. The fix was one switch. The more useful change was to the script: it now reports the HTTP status and the first bytes of what it received, instead of collapsing a challenge page, a 404 and a dead tunnel into the same word. A failure message that cannot distinguish its causes is a bug in the failure message.
It is the one gap in the table above.
In-cluster monitoring goes dark with the cluster; a probe on a Worker cron does not.
Move content authoring into the CMS and publish through it,
so that the pipeline above is triggered by a publish rather than by a commit.
Cache the HTML at the edge.
Today every page view reaches the homelab; the cache purge on publish is already in place.

title.en: How this site is built: a static blog on a homelab

description.en: A headless CMS, a static Astro build, and nginx pods that keep serving even when the CMS is down. The reasoning and the trade-offs.

children.text: Astro build. The words live in a headless CMS, but readers never touch it: they get plain files from
(or from a mirror in object storage when the homelab is down).
Publishing in the CMS triggers a build. The build produces a
folder, uploads it as a numbered release, and moves a pointer. The pods notice the new pointer and swap their content without a rollout.

Why not just render pages from the CMS?
a static file keeps working when the database does not.
no application runtime on the read path.
the CMS is only reachable behind an access gate.
A static site on a single-house homelab is strictly less available than a hosted static platform. The point of running it here is to learn, which is why a failover mirror exists.
The schema is code. Types generated from it are imported by the site, so a schema change that breaks a page fails the type check before it fails a reader.

title.en: TraderBuddy architecture: the stack and the constraints behind it

description.en: What TraderBuddy is made of, and the constraints that shaped it: one WebSocket, thirty symbols, SIP versus IEX, and alerts that need previous state.

children.text: What the system is made of, and the handful of constraints that explain why it is shaped this way rather than some more obvious way.

A self-hosted trading dashboard for about five people: live quotes, server-computed indicators, drawing tools, price alerts delivered to Slack, macro context, and a manual portfolio tracker. It runs on a three-node Talos cluster on Proxmox, behind Cloudflare.
It tracks and alerts. It never trades.

There is no order entry, no broker connection, no paper trading — even though the charting frontend is forked from a project that had all three. The portfolio is a manual ledger you type into. This is a product decision, not a missing feature.

fields.alt: Component architecture: the browser reaches Cloudflare, then a Cilium Gateway API route, which splits traffic between tb-web and tb-api. tb-api talks to Postgres, Valkey, Zitadel and market-data providers. tb-stream holds the single upstream Alpaca WebSocket; tb-alerts and tb-ingest run as scheduled jobs.

children.text: Components and the traffic between them.
Async throughout because most request time is provider I/O.
Vite 6, React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Query, zustand
A fork of OpenCharts (MIT), pruned to charting only.
on — Apache-2.0 attribution is a licence condition, not a preference.
Pinned to v8 on purpose; see "Deliberate deviations" below.
Everything durable. Sessions and queues included.
Short-TTL caching and rate-limit buckets only. Nothing here is a source of truth.
The browser holds an opaque signed cookie. No JWT ever reaches it.
Computed in Python only. The frontend never calculates.
Alpaca (bars, quotes, news, corporate actions), Finnhub (fundamentals, earnings), FRED + Shiller (macro)
All free tiers. All keys server-side.
Talos v1.14, Kubernetes v1.36, Cilium v1.20 Gateway API
Gateway API, not Ingress and not Traefik.
The Python codebase ships as a single
image with four entrypoints. Each Deployment runs a different
. There are deliberately not four backend images.
Holds the single upstream Alpaca WebSocket and republishes to Valkey pub/sub
Evaluates price alerts after the close
Symbols, bar retention, macro, portfolio snapshots, digest, scan
WebSocket connection per account and 30 subscribed symbols. That single fact produces most of the streaming design:
, because two pods briefly coexisting means a
and no live prices for anyone.
in symbols; a budget allocator picks which 30 get the live feed, holding a symbol for 60 seconds after interest drops so a tab switch doesn't thrash subscriptions.
Symbols outside the budget are polled from a cached snapshot about every 15 seconds and labelled
in the UI rather than silently shown as live.

fields.alt: Streaming dataflow: tb-stream holds one Alpaca WebSocket, publishes ticks and bars to Valkey pub/sub; each tb-api replica subscribes and fans out to browser WebSocket connections, with delayed symbols served from a polled snapshot cache.

children.text: One upstream connection, fanned out through Valkey to every browser.
Real-time is IEX; history is SIP
Live quotes come from IEX, which is a few percent of US volume. Historical bars come from SIP, which is consolidated and authoritative — but the free plan
embargoes the last 15 minutes of SIP
falls inside that window rather than trimming it.
clear of the window for that reason.

The consequence users see: an intraday chart can disagree with an alert until the close, because alerts evaluate SIP bars afterwards. The UI labels which feed a chart is showing instead of pretending they're the same.
(a moving-average cross, a new high, a volume spike, RSI, a percent move) answer a question about a whole session rather than watching 1-minute bars for a touch, so they take their own path:

is pure — daily bars in, a verdict out — and calls the same pandas-ta functions that draw the chart's indicators, so an alert cannot disagree with the line the user is looking at. Daily bars are fetched split-adjusted; level alerts stay on raw prices because a level is a raw price. A condition has no price, so

is nullable, held honest by CHECK constraints, and the chart never draws a line for one. A cross is two consecutive sessions on opposite sides of the line, which is where "previous state" comes from without storing any.

. That distinction requires knowing the previous close, which is why alerts are evaluated once per trading day, server-side, on the session's SIP 1-minute bars — never on ticks, never in the browser. Dragging an alert line past the current price doesn't fire it: the baseline resets and only bars after the edit count.
Money is Decimal, and strings on the wire
is a float to every client. The frontend formats them and does no arithmetic on them.
This is not pedantry. The portfolio ledger's property-based test caught a real bug this way:

round differently once average cost is a repeating decimal, and the books failed to balance by one ulp. Replay now quantizes to the column precisions, so what it computes is exactly what Postgres stores.
Portfolios, alerts and watchlists are scoped to the session user — someone else's id returns

, so the API never confirms which ids exist. Notifications go only to destinations that user connected themselves — their own Slack (a direct message, or a channel they choose), Telegram chat or webhook. The

refuses anything but a DM, because a channel would show every user everyone else's holdings. A user-owned Slack token is different — workspace, app and destination are all theirs — so it may post to a channel they pick, and the UI says plainly that everyone in it can read the alerts.
Zitadel authenticates; TraderBuddy authorizes. Registration is open, but every new user is
until an admin approves them — over HTTP and over the WebSocket, which authenticates separately and needed its own check.
is off in Zitadel precisely so a newcomer gets a waiting screen rather than an error page. The
role still comes from Zitadel's project-role claim.
Slack and Telegram tokens and webhook URLs are encrypted at rest with Fernet (

), as a whole blob rather than selected fields, because a webhook URL can carry a token in its path. The API is write-only for them — nothing returns a credential, so there is no "show token" — and no admin route touches the table. Webhooks are the one feature that lets a user aim the server at an address of their choosing, in a cluster that also runs Zitadel, Postgres and the Kubernetes API, and

, so the guard is the only defence: HTTPS only, every resolved address checked, then the connection made to the address that was checked rather than the name (a second DNS lookup would allow rebinding), no redirects.
The one exception, decided 2026-10-03: a user holding the Zitadel
role can read any user's watchlist and portfolios, and a
. It is read-only, it 404s for everyone else, and it carries two conditions — every cross-user read writes an
row, and the settings dialog tells
user this is possible. Searches are not logged anywhere.
. The session cookie resolves against a
Zitadel is never called on a normal request
— no introspection endpoint — because it runs a single replica and would be a hard dependency on every page load. Roles are a snapshot taken at login and refreshed on token refresh.
. Fan-out through Valkey is what lets
scale to two replicas while only one upstream connection exists.

reads closed bars from the Postgres cache, backfills from Alpaca only when the newest cached bar could be stale, and appends one live forming bar from IEX in two narrow cases. Closed bars are immutable once written.
A coding agent speaks MCP to

. A door in front of the mount checks the token (SHA-256 lookup in Postgres; Zitadel is never involved) and each tool then calls the app's own REST routes in-process, carrying the same token. So validation, the approval gate, per-user scoping and rate limits are the browser's, not a copy of them. A token user has no roles, and what a token may reach is a fail-closed method-and-path allowlist in
fetches split-adjusted SIP daily bars for the shared universe (S&P 500, a few Nasdaq-100 extras,

100 curated ETFs) plus every symbol anyone watches or holds, computes the moving averages, RSI, highs, volume and cross events once per symbol with the same pandas-ta calls the chart uses, joins cached Finnhub fundamentals, and writes one

row each. It is all-or-nothing: if a fetch fails the previous night's snapshot stands. Scans read that table and never a provider. Fundamentals are refreshed 150 symbols a night, paced under half the shared Finnhub budget, so they are up to a week old.
A scan is a validated list of filters (
) compiled to SQL from a field whitelist, so no string a user sends is ever an identifier. Each query is restricted to
is_core OR symbol IN (your watchlist and holdings)

: the snapshot contains rows that exist only because one person holds a symbol, and they must never appear for anyone else. "New" is computed by running the same filters on the previous session's snapshot, which is kept for two weeks, so there is no extra table.
Once the snapshot is committed the same job sends each user's notifying scanners (
on is run through the same
as the page, so the privacy restriction is identical, and the matches go out as one message through
to that user's own channels. A
row is claimed per user per session before sending, as the digest does, so a rerun never posts twice; a send that fails everywhere releases the claim for the retry.
Statements come from SEC EDGAR, which is free and keyless and which the browser never calls. Every request carries a
naming a project contact address, and goes through a Valkey token bucket at 8 requests a second (the SEC allows 10) shared by both API replicas and the nightly job. For a symbol,
serves a stored report younger than a day; otherwise it reads the company's small submissions list and recomputes only when a new filing accession has appeared or the scoring
changed. A recompute parses the multi-megabyte
30 concepts we map and drops the rest before the next company.

Companies tag the same line differently and change tags over time, so each field takes the first mapped tag that has a value for each period; annual figures are 345–385-day facts with the latest filing winning restatements, and trailing twelve months is the last fiscal year plus this year's year-to-date minus last year's. Indicators and the score are pure functions (

): a piecewise-linear table per indicator, a pillar is the mean of its indicators, and the overall score is the weighted mean of the pillars that could be scored. Unknown is never zero — a missing input is skipped, and fewer than three scored pillars is no score. The report is stored in
block; the nightly scan reads only that block in SQL, never the whole report, which is the memory lesson from 0.4.3. If the SEC is unreachable the stored report is served marked stale.
Each of these is a place the implementation diverged from
on purpose. They are recorded here because an undocumented deviation reads as a bug to the next person.
Profile, metrics and recommendations have identical shape and TTL. Three identical tables would be three places to change.
Hides the candles, adds a baseline series
The drawing manager, crosshair legend and bid/ask lines all hold a reference to the candle series. Removing it would leave them pointing at a disposed object.
v9 is a ground-up redesign (atom stores, a
HOC). A sortable positions table isn't worth guessing at an unfamiliar API.
Fall back to the last regular-session 1-minute bar if the SIP daily close includes extended hours

extended hours. AAPL printed above its regular high after the bell and the daily bar still matched the regular session exactly. The daily close is the official consolidated close — the fallback would have been a downgrade.
Watchlist truncated when the Slack block budget runs short
1,600 rows. The cap exists because a DM listing forty symbols is unreadable.
is a single point of failure.
The free tier offers no fix. It is monitored, not solved.
— etcd majority and two of three Postgres instances. The real fix is a third host, which doesn't exist.
Provider free tiers can change without notice.
The provider layer is built so swapping one is a config change.
A sixth may need paid tiers, not more RAM.
Analyst consensus is opinion data; indicator crossings are not predictions.
Last updated 2026-10-06. The diagrams above are drawn from D2 source files kept with the project.

description.en: A self-hosted terminal for the US market: server-side indicators, after-close alerts, a screener, SEC financials and a manual portfolio. It never trades.

children.text: It tracks and alerts. It never trades.
A self-hosted terminal for the US market: charts with every indicator computed on the server, alerts that reach your own Slack or Telegram after the close, a screener over
600 symbols, company financials read straight from SEC filings, and a portfolio you keep by hand. No broker connection, no order entry, and nothing about you sold to anyone.

fields.title: An example TraderBuddy chart: daily candles with a server-computed moving average, a price alert level drawn at 230 with its bell enabled, and a dashed average-cost line at 214 for a symbol held in a portfolio.
fields.caption: One symbol, as the chart shows it: candles, a server-computed moving average, an alert armed at 230, and the dashed line marking what you paid. An illustration with example prices.

children.text: Open a symbol and you get candles from one minute to one week, drawn from closed bars cached on the server with one live forming bar on top. Scroll back and deeper history loads.
SMA, EMA, RSI, ATR, VWAP, MACD, Bollinger Bands and Stochastic. Your browser draws them; it never calculates them, so the chart and an alert can never disagree.
Trendlines, horizontals, rectangles and text, with magnet snapping, undo and redo, and an object tree. Everything is saved per symbol and waiting when you come back.
Real-time prices stream for the symbols you have open. The rest are polled and labelled
, so you always know which number you are looking at.
Show closes against a reference instead of in absolute terms: since you added the symbol, 1W, 1M, 3M, YTD or 1Y. The legend names the reference price and its date.
Info and news beside the chart.
Profile, P/E, P/B, dividend yield, beta, a 52-week range bar and analyst ratings, marked as opinion. News follows your watchlist and falls back to market news when it is empty.
A dashed average-cost line on the chart and a dot in the watchlist, so a position never gets lost between pages.
adds it to your watchlist. What you type is never logged.
The chart keeps the screen. Indicators, Draw, Watchlist, News and Info are named buttons underneath, and the page tabs sit along the bottom.

Draw a line where you care about the price, turn on its bell, and TraderBuddy watches that level for you. Or create one from the Alerts page, where every alert you own is listed, editable, renewable and deletable.

fields.title: How an alert travels: your alert, then after the US close the session’s one-minute bars are read once a day, and only if the previous close sat on the other side of your level does a message go to the channels you connected.
fields.caption: How an alert reaches you, and the one rule that decides whether it fires.

children.text: The timing is the part worth knowing before you rely on it: alerts are checked
once per trading day, after the US close

, on that session's one-minute bars. That is a deliberate trade — the real-time budget belongs to the charts you have open — and it means an alert tells you on the evening of the day something happened, not the second it happens. The single exception is opening movers, below.
Crosses above, below, or either. On a trendline, the level is read along the line at the moment of checking, so a sloping level stays correct as time passes.

A close crossing its SMA or EMA, a golden or death cross, a daily move of X%, a new 52-week or all-time high or low, a volume spike, or RSI crossing a level. Any symbol in the universe, ETFs included.
A condition alert says what occurred rather than quoting a number: "the 50-day crossed above the 200-day", not "value
A Slack DM, a Slack channel you pick, a Telegram chat, or a signed webhook. Every enabled channel gets every alert, and one failing never costs you the others.
Alerts last 90 days and then wait for you to renew them, re-arm after they fire, and keep a per-alert history of what happened and when. Renew or delete in bulk.
The chart agrees with the server.
A bell on the chart means a real alert exists on the server. You will never be shown one that isn't actually armed.

Filter about 600 symbols — the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 names, roughly 100 ETFs, plus anything on your own watchlist or in your portfolio — on price moves, the 52-week range, volume against its average, SMA 20/50/200, RSI, golden and death crosses, new highs and lows, P/E, market cap and financial health. Thirteen scans are built in. Duplicate one to edit it, or save up to 25 of your own.
As of the close, Fri 9 Oct 2026
S&P 500 — the 500 largest US listed companies.
above 7% or below −7% — a move far outside a normal session.
above 2× its 20-day average — unusual participation, not a quiet drift.
and twelve more S&P 500 names moved 7% or more that session
A real match: Moderna's 8–9 October spike, caught by a 7% move scan and a 2× volume scan.
Every scanner explains itself as you build it: "Debt / equity: below 1× — total debt over equity; under 1 is a lighter balance sheet." You can add a description in your own words.
Results are a snapshot taken after each close, and the page says which close. Symbols that were not matching the session before are marked
— new matches only, or every match — and one message per evening lists what each of your scanners found, every symbol linking to its chart. Nothing is sent on a day nothing matched.
A symbol whose value is unknown — no 200-day average yet, no P/E — never matches a filter on it, instead of being quietly counted as zero.
Search a company and TraderBuddy reads its latest 10-K or 10-Q from the SEC, names the filing it used, links to it, and turns it into one score with the five parts behind it.

fields.title: An example financial health score of 78 out of 100, broken into five pillars drawn on the same scale: profitability 86, cash flow 81, balance sheet 74, shareholders 68 and growth 52.
fields.caption: A financial health score and the five parts behind it, all on the same 0–100 scale. Example figures.

children.text: Each indicator carries its value, a five-year trend, a good / fair / weak marker and one plain explanation: "Out of every $100 of revenue, $23 is left after the direct costs."
Two checks shown test by test.
The Piotroski F-score's nine pass/fail tests and the Altman Z-score's safe, grey or distress zones, each displayed in full so the score is never a black box.
Five years of income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, in line names a person recognises.
A figure the filing does not report is left out. A part without enough data says so, and a company with too little to go on gets no score at all.
For banks and insurers the measures that do not apply are dropped rather than invented, and the page says which and why.
The score summarises what a company reported about its past. It does not forecast the share price, and the page says so plainly.

A ledger you keep yourself: buys, sells, dividends, splits and fees, typed in or imported from CSV with a preview and per-row errors first. There is no broker connection, by choice. Positions, profit and loss, and history are all derived by replaying what you entered.

fields.title: An example portfolio chart with two lines from nightly snapshots: market value rising to 16,480 dollars and cost basis stepping from 10,000 to 14,000 dollars in the month money was added, so a deposit cannot be mistaken for a return.
fields.caption: Value against cost from nightly snapshots. Example figures.

children.text: Money and quantities are exact decimals end to end, never floating point. Every edit replays the whole ledger, so a backdated sell that would oversell is refused and names the transaction it conflicts with.
Positions use average cost rather than tax lots, and the interface tells you that instead of letting you assume otherwise.
By symbol or by sector, with
shown rather than hidden when a sector isn't available.
Splits and dividends that look unrecorded are pointed out, and "Record it" pre-fills the transaction. Nothing is ever applied to your ledger automatically.

Eight series on one page: the 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields, the 10y−2y spread, the Fed funds rate, CPI, unemployment, the VIX and the Shiller CAPE. Every figure shows the observation date it belongs to, because a macro number without its date reads as today's when it can be months old.
Colour follows meaning rather than direction, and stops where meaning stops:
Worse — more joblessness, faster inflation, more stress, a more expensive starting point
through zero that people watch as a recession signal
Neutral — higher rates are good for savers and bad for borrowers; picking a colour would be editorialising
A daily digest, if you want one
Off until you turn it on, section by section. After the close on trading days, you get one message on the channels you connected, with any section that has nothing to say left out.
An example of how it arrives
Core · +$412 today, value $16,480 against $14,000 of cost.
AAPL crossed above 230.00. The alert has re-armed.
Three headlines on symbols you follow, and who reports tomorrow.
It is sent at most once a day. A crash can make it skip a day; it can never send you the same day twice.
One hour after the US open, TraderBuddy looks for S&P 500 stocks running: up
on yesterday's close and trading at least
for those first minutes, measured against the same minutes of the last ten sessions, because volume is always heaviest at the open.
An example of how it arrives
Two S&P 500 names are running an hour into the session.
+6.4% on 3.1× its usual volume for this part of the morning.
This is the one thing in TraderBuddy that runs

the session, and it is a deliberate exception. It is off until you turn it on in Settings, next to the digest. It arrives on trading days only, at most once a day, and never on a quiet morning. The time is shown in your own time zone, and the message says plainly that its prices are the full-market feed, 15 minutes delayed.
Let a coding agent use it

Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients can look symbols up and manage your alerts, watchlist and drawings on your behalf. Create a token in Settings, paste the URL into your client, and ask in words:
"what is NVDA's RSI doing, and alert me if it crosses 70"

A token is shown once, expires between 30 days and a year, and is revoked rather than deleted. It can be read-only or allowed to write alerts, your watchlist, drawings and digest settings. What it can never touch is fixed in the server, not in the client: your notification credentials, the admin area, your portfolio ledger, and minting more tokens. And since TraderBuddy has no order entry at all, no agent of yours can place a trade.
Your browser talks to one server.
Only TraderBuddy's own. No analytics, no third-party widgets, no market-data provider called from your machine. Every provider key stays server-side.
Nothing logs what you type into ⌘K or the symbol box. Not for you, not for an admin.
Every portfolio, alert and watchlist route is scoped to you; someone else's id simply does not exist. Notifications go to destinations you connected yourself, never a shared channel.
Slack and Telegram tokens and webhook secrets are encrypted at rest and never returned by any route, to you or to anyone. To change one you replace it.

An admin can read any user's watchlist, portfolios and alerts — read-only. Every such read is recorded in an audit log, and the app tells every user this is possible. Your searches still aren't logged, and your channel credentials stay out of reach.
Anyone can register; nobody gets in until an admin approves them. Until then you see a waiting screen and nothing else.
What it deliberately does not do
These are choices, not gaps, and they are not going to change:
No order entry, no broker positions, no depth of market, no paper trading.
The portfolio is typed in or imported from a CSV.
Average cost only, and it says so where it matters.
Once per trading day, after the close.
Indicators, crossings and signals are all server-side.
Analyst consensus is opinion data, an indicator crossing is not a prediction, and a financial score is a summary of past filings.
Features as of version 0.7.0, 11 October 2026. Example figures are illustrations, not real data.
